It was a strange sight: a tiny girl with dark hair, with her feet nowhere near the floor, lost in the wonderful adventures of Pip and old Miss Havisham and her house full of cobwebs. She was also held by the magic that Dickens, the great story-teller, had made with his words. The only movement was her hand, which now and then turned a page. paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Trunchbull is a huge and fierce woman. Everyone is afraid of her, and the writer says we should keep away from people like her.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Trunchbull, the Headmistress, was not like Miss Honey at all. She was a huge, terrible person, a fierce monster who ruled by fear. Pupils and teachers were both very afraid of her. Even from far away you felt that she was dangerous. When she came close, you could almost feel heat coming from her, like heat from a red-hot rod of metal. Miss Trunchbull never walked. She marched, like a soldier, with long steps and her arms swinging. When she marched along a corridor, you could hear her snorting. If some children were in her way, she went right through them like a tank, and the small people bounced off her to the left and the right. The writer says we are lucky that we do not meet many people like her. But they do live in the world, and each of us will probably meet at least one in a life. If you do, you should do what you would do if you met a very angry rhinoceros in the bush. Climb the nearest tree and stay there until it has gone away. This woman is very strange in her ways and in how she looks, and it is almost impossible to describe her.

paragraphs.context: words like child-genius and prodigy went flitting through her head
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Honey thinks Matilda has a very special brain for numbers. She remembers that Mozart began to write music at five.
paragraphs.simple: 'You are right,' Miss Honey said. 'Anyway, pocket calculators are not allowed in this school.' Miss Honey felt shaky. She was sure that she had met a truly special child with a brain for numbers. Words like child-genius and prodigy went quickly through her head. She knew that such wonders come into the world now and then, but only once or twice in a hundred years. She thought of Mozart. He was only five when he began to write music for the piano, and look at what happened to him.

paragraphs.context: She had an obstinate chin, a cruel mouth and small arrogant eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: This paragraph tells how strong Miss Trunchbull looks and what strange clothes she wears.
paragraphs.simple: Above all, she was a very strong woman who made people afraid. She had once been a famous athlete, and you could still clearly see her muscles. They were in her thick neck like a bull's, her big shoulders, her thick arms, her strong thin wrists and her powerful legs. When you looked at her, you felt that she could bend iron bars and tear telephone books in half. Her face was not beautiful. She had a hard chin, a cruel mouth and small, proud eyes. Her clothes were very strange. She always wore a brown cotton smock, tight at the waist with a wide leather belt. The belt had a huge silver buckle in front. Her big thighs came out of the smock into a pair of strange trousers, bottle-green in colour and made of rough cloth. They came down to just below the knees. Below them she wore green stockings with turned-over tops, which showed her leg muscles very well. On her feet she had flat brown leather shoes with flaps. The writer says she looked more like a strange, cruel person who hunts with dogs than like the head of a nice school for children.

paragraphs.context: Squashing a bad girl is like trying to squash a bluebottle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Trunchbull is sure that Matilda put a stink-bomb under her desk. She says bad girls are worse than bad boys.
paragraphs.simple: 'Oh yes, Miss Honey, it is right!' said Miss Trunchbull. 'Now that I think of it, I am sure that she put that stink-bomb under my desk this morning. The room smelled like a sewer! Of course it was her! I will punish her for that, you will see! What does she look like? A nasty little worm, I am sure. In my long years as a teacher I have learned this: a bad girl is much more dangerous than a bad boy. Also, bad girls are much harder to stop. Trying to squash a bad girl is like trying to squash a bluebottle. You bang down on it and it is not there. Little girls are nasty, dirty things. I am glad I was never one.'
hardWords: I shall have her for that

paragraphs.context: She simply refused to let the matter rest where it was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Honey decides to go and talk to Matilda's parents in secret. She is sure she can tell them how special Matilda is, but she thinks it will be hard to stop them from getting too excited.
paragraphs.simple: At the same time, Miss Honey was making another decision. She would go herself, as soon as she could, and talk in private with Matilda's mother and father. She would not leave the matter as it was. It was all silly. She could not believe that the parents did not know about their daughter's wonderful gifts. Mr Wormwood was a successful car dealer, so she thought he must be a fairly clever man. Also, parents never thought their own children were less able than they really were. It was the other way round. Sometimes it was almost impossible for a teacher to make proud parents see that their loved child was a complete fool. Miss Honey was sure it would be easy to tell Mr and Mrs Wormwood that Matilda was very special. She thought the problem would be how to stop them from getting too excited.
hardWords: refused to let the matter rest

paragraphs.context: brought the art of skulduggery to the highest point of perfection
paragraphs.mainIdea: Matilda and Lavender think Hortensia is a great hero. Even the boil on her nose looks like a sign of courage.
paragraphs.simple: Matilda and Lavender were held by her story. They felt they were standing in front of a master. Here was a person who had made the art of playing tricks as good as it could be. She was also willing to risk her life and body for what she loved to do. They looked at this goddess with wonder. All at once, even the boil on her nose was not ugly any more. It was a sign of courage.

paragraphs.context: flung him clear out of the open classroom window
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hortensia tells a story about Miss Trunchbull throwing a boy out of a window for eating sweets in class.
paragraphs.simple: 'Listen to this,' Hortensia said. 'Only yesterday the Trunchbull saw a boy called Julius Rottwinkle eating Liquorice Allsorts in the scripture lesson. She picked him up by one arm and threw him right out of the open classroom window. Our classroom is one floor up. We saw Julius Rottwinkle fly out over the garden like a Frisbee and land with a thump in the middle of the lettuces. Then the Trunchbull turned to us and said, "From now on, anybody caught eating in class goes straight out the window."'

paragraphs.context: The Trunchbull was not a person who would give someone a whole chocolate cake
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bruce Bogtrotter stops before he cuts the cake. All the children think there is something bad in it.
paragraphs.simple: The boy picked up the knife. He was going to cut the cake, but he stopped. He looked hard at the cake. Then he looked up at the Trunchbull, and then at the tall thin cook with her lemon-juice mouth. All the children in the hall watched, tense, waiting for something to happen. They were sure that it would. The Trunchbull was not a person who would give someone a whole chocolate cake just to be kind. Many of them guessed that it was full of pepper, or castor-oil, or something else that tastes foul and would make the boy very sick. It might even be arsenic, and he would be dead in ten seconds. Or perhaps it was a cake with a hidden bomb, and it would blow up as soon as it was cut, and Bruce Bogtrotter with it. Nobody in the school thought the Trunchbull would not do any of these things.

paragraphs.context: It is an incredibly ugly gruesome-looking animal, rather like a baby crocodile
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lavender finds a newt. The paragraph tells what a newt is like.
paragraphs.simple: At the bottom of Lavender's garden there was a muddy pond. A group of newts lived in it. In English ponds the newt is quite common, but ordinary people do not often see it, because it is a shy and dark animal. It is a very ugly animal that looks horrible, a bit like a baby crocodile but with a shorter head. It does not hurt anyone, but it does not look like that. It is about six inches long and very slimy. On top its skin is greenish-grey, and underneath its belly is orange. It is an amphibian, so it can live in water or out of water.

paragraphs.context: In this room there was an enormous human bomb in front of them
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children watch Miss Trunchbull as if she might explode. She says she does not like small people.
paragraphs.simple: Rupert got up and went back to his desk. He rubbed his head with both hands. The Trunchbull went back to the front of the class. The children sat still, as if they could not move. None of them had seen anything like this before. It was very good to watch, better than a pantomime, but with one big difference. In this room, in front of them, there was a huge human bomb that might go off at any moment and blow someone to pieces. The children could not look away from the Headmistress. 'I don't like small people,' she was saying. 'Nobody should ever see small people. They should be kept out of sight in boxes, like hairpins and buttons. I cannot understand why children take so long to grow up. I think they do it on purpose.'

paragraphs.context: A kind of electricity seemed to be gathering inside them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Matilda feels a strange power in her eyes. It feels like electricity and lightning.
paragraphs.simple: The Trunchbull sat behind the teacher's table. She stared at the newt in the glass, with fear and with great interest. Matilda's eyes were fixed on the glass too. Slowly, a very strange feeling began to come over Matilda. The feeling was mostly in her eyes. It seemed that a kind of electricity was gathering inside them. A feeling of power, of great strength, was growing deep in her eyes. There was another feeling too, which was different, and she could not understand it. It was like flashes of lightning. Little waves of lightning seemed to flash out of her eyes. Her eyeballs began to get hot, as if a huge amount of energy was building up inside them. It was an amazing feeling. She kept her eyes on the glass. Now the power was coming together in one small part of each eye. It grew stronger and stronger. It felt as if millions of tiny invisible arms with hands on them were shooting out of her eyes towards the glass.

paragraphs.context: The room was as small and square and bare as a prison cell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Matilda sees that the sitting-room in Miss Honey's cottage has almost nothing in it.
paragraphs.simple: 'Let's have it in the sitting-room,' Miss Honey said. She picked up the tray and led the way out of the kitchen, down the dark little tunnel, to the room at the front. Matilda followed her. But just inside the door of the so-called sitting-room, she stopped and looked around in great surprise. The room was as small, square and bare as a prison cell. The pale light came from one tiny window in the front wall, and there were no curtains. The only things in the whole room were two wooden boxes turned upside down to be chairs, and a third box between them to be a table. That was all. There were no pictures on the walls and no carpet on the floor. There were only rough wooden planks, with gaps between them where dust and dirt had collected. The ceiling was so low that Matilda could nearly touch it with her fingertips if she jumped. The walls were white, but it did not look like paint. Matilda rubbed her hand on it, and white powder came off on her skin. It was whitewash, the cheap stuff that people use in cowsheds, stables and hen-houses.

paragraphs.context: I became so completely cowed and dominated by this monster of an aunt
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Honey says she was so afraid of her aunt that she did everything her aunt told her. By ten she was her aunt's slave.
paragraphs.simple: 'Of course,' Miss Honey said. 'I went to the same school that you go to now. But I lived at home.' Miss Honey stopped and looked down into her empty tea-mug. 'I think what I am trying to tell you,' she said, 'is that over the years I became so afraid of this monster of an aunt, and she ruled me so much, that I did what she said at once, whatever it was. That can happen, you know. By the time I was ten, I was her slave. I did all the housework. I made her bed. I washed and ironed her clothes. I did all the cooking. I learned how to do everything.'

paragraphs.context: as though she had touched something that was not quite of this world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Matilda feels very happy and strong after the chalk wrote by itself. It all seemed very easy.
paragraphs.simple: Matilda sat still at her desk. She felt strangely happy and excited. She felt as if she had touched something not quite from this world: the highest point of the sky, the farthest star. She had felt the power rush up behind her eyes, like a warm liquid pouring inside her head. Her eyes had become hotter than ever before. Things had come bursting out of her eye-sockets, and then the piece of chalk had lifted itself up and begun to write. It seemed that she had hardly done anything. It had all been so easy.

paragraphs.context: the last will and testament of her late father, Dr Honey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Honey gets a letter from lawyers. It says she owns The Red House and her father's money.
paragraphs.simple: On the second morning, Miss Honey got a letter by registered post from a firm of local lawyers. It said that the last will of her dead father, Dr Honey, had suddenly turned up in a strange way. The will showed that since her father died, Miss Honey had really owned a house at the edge of the village called The Red House. Until a short time ago, a Miss Agatha Trunchbull had lived in it. The will also showed that her father had left her all the money he had saved in his life. Luckily, it was still safe in the bank. The lawyer's letter said that if Miss Honey would come to the office as soon as she could, the house and the money could be put in her name very quickly.

paragraphs.context: somebody's probably tipped him off that the police are on to him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Honey tells Matilda why her father is running away. He sold stolen cars and now the police know.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Honey went on, 'People brought stolen cars to your father's workshop. There he changed the number-plates and sprayed the cars a different colour, and did all the rest of it. Now someone has probably told him in secret that the police know about him. He is doing what they all do. He is running away to Spain, where the police cannot get him. He will have been sending his money there for years, all ready for when he arrives.'

sentences.context: It is only when the parents begin telling us about the brilliance
sentences.simple: We only start to shout when parents tell us how clever their awful children are. Then we shout, "Bring us a basin! We're going to be sick!"
sentences.grammar: 'It is only when ... that ...' puts the focus on the time: we shout at that time and not before.

sentences.context: If I were a teacher I would cook up some real scorchers
sentences.simple: If he were a teacher, he would write some very hard reports for the children of parents who love their children too much.
sentences.grammar: 'If I were + would + verb' is an imagined case; people use 'were' for 'I' in this kind of 'if' sentence.

sentences.context: I doubt they would have noticed had she crawled into the house
sentences.simple: The writer thinks they would not have seen it, even if she had crawled into the house with a broken leg.
sentences.grammar: 'had she crawled' means 'if she had crawled'; the 'if' is dropped and 'had' goes first. 'would have noticed' tells about a past case that did not happen.

sentences.context: Her mind was so nimble and she was so quick to learn that her ability should have been obvious
sentences.simple: Her mind was very quick and she learned very fast. So even her parents should have seen how clever she was.
sentences.grammar: 'so ... that ...' shows a result; 'should have been' says something was expected in the past but did not happen.

sentences.context: small girls should be seen and not heard
sentences.simple: The parents called her a noisy chatterbox. They told her sharply that small girls should be seen but not heard.
sentences.grammar: 'should be seen' is a passive with 'should' (what is right to do); 'seen and not heard' is an old saying.

sentences.context: when she had read this from cover to cover and had learnt all the recipes by heart
sentences.simple: She read the book from the first page to the last and learned all the recipes. After that she decided she wanted something more interesting.
sentences.grammar: 'had read' and 'had learnt' are past perfect: they happened before 'she decided'.

sentences.context: And a strange sight it was, this tiny dark-haired person sitting there
sentences.simple: It was a strange thing to see: a tiny girl with dark hair sitting there, with her feet nowhere near the floor. She was lost in the adventures of Pip and old Miss Havisham, and in the magic that Dickens made with his words.
sentences.grammar: The words 'a strange sight' are put first for effect; the normal order is 'It was a strange sight.' 'sitting there' is a participle phrase about the person.

sentences.context: Almost anyone else witnessing the achievements of this small child would have been tempted
sentences.simple: Almost any other person who saw what this small child did would have wanted to make a big fuss and shout the news all over the village. But Mrs Phelps was not like that.
sentences.grammar: 'witnessing ...' is a participle phrase that tells which person (= anyone who witnessed); 'would have been tempted' says what that person would have felt.

sentences.context: impossible to tamper with it unless you're a ruddy watchmaker
sentences.simple: The car makers have fixed it so that nobody can change it, unless the person is a watchmaker or something like that.
sentences.grammar: 'unless' means 'if ... not': it is impossible to change it, except when you are a watchmaker.

sentences.context: Well, if I were to run the car backwards for long enough then obviously that would do it
sentences.simple: Mr Wormwood says that if he ran the car backwards for long enough, that would obviously do it.
sentences.grammar: 'if I were to + verb' talks about an imagined case; the result uses 'would'.

sentences.context: is run off a cable that is coupled up to one of the front wheels
sentences.simple: The speedometer works from a cable. The cable is joined to one of the front wheels.
sentences.grammar: 'is run' and 'is coupled' are passive; 'that' starts a relative clause that tells which cable.

sentences.context: If only they would read a little Dickens or Kipling they would soon discover
sentences.simple: Matilda wishes her parents would read some Dickens or Kipling. Then they would soon find out that life is more than cheating people and watching television.
sentences.grammar: 'If only + would' shows a strong wish about something that may not happen; the result clause uses 'would'.

sentences.context: Superglue is very powerful stuff, so powerful it will take your skin off
sentences.simple: Superglue is very strong. It is so strong that it will take your skin off if you pull too hard.
sentences.grammar: 'so powerful (that) ...' shows a result; the word 'that' has been left out.

sentences.context: The only sensible thing to do when you are attacked is, as Napoleon once said, to counter-attack
sentences.simple: When someone attacks you, the only sensible thing is to attack back. Napoleon once said this.
sentences.grammar: 'to counter-attack' is an infinitive after 'is'; 'as Napoleon once said' is an extra part put inside the sentence.

sentences.context: depended, however, upon whether or not Fred's parrot was really as good a talker as Fred made out
sentences.simple: Her plan depended on one thing. Was Fred's parrot really as good at talking as Fred said?
sentences.grammar: 'whether or not' starts a noun clause (it means 'if it was true or not'); 'as good a talker as' is the 'as ... as' comparison with a noun.

sentences.context: however asinine the orders might be
sentences.simple: She always had to do what she was told, even when the orders were very silly.
sentences.grammar: 'however + adjective + subject + verb' means 'no matter how ...'; 'might' shows it could be so.

sentences.context: the thing that prevented her from going round the bend
sentences.simple: The thing that stopped her from going mad was the fun of making up punishments.
sentences.grammar: 'that prevented her' is a relative clause; 'prevent someone from + -ing' means to stop someone doing something.

sentences.context: of which he was exceedingly proud
sentences.simple: Mr Wormwood had a lot of black hair. He parted it in the middle and he was very proud of it.
sentences.grammar: 'of which' starts a relative clause and replaces 'it' after 'proud of': he was proud of his hair.

sentences.context: If you get on the wrong side of Miss Trunchbull she can liquidise you
sentences.simple: If you make Miss Trunchbull angry, she can turn you into liquid, like a carrot in a kitchen blender.
sentences.grammar: 'If + present, can + verb' is a real case: if one thing happens, the other can happen.

sentences.context: She had never come across a five-year-old before, or indeed a ten-year-old, who could multiply
sentences.simple: Miss Honey had never met a five-year-old, or even a ten-year-old, who could multiply like this.
sentences.grammar: 'had never come across' is past perfect and means 'before that time'; 'who could multiply' tells about the child.

sentences.context: you should behave as you would if you met an enraged rhinoceros
sentences.simple: If you ever meet a person like her, do what you would do if you met a very angry rhinoceros in the bush. Climb the nearest tree and stay there until it has gone away.
sentences.grammar: 'as you would if you met ...' compares with an imagined case: 'if + past' and 'would'.

sentences.context: how she ever got her present job was a mystery
sentences.simple: Nobody could understand how she got her job as head teacher.
sentences.grammar: 'how she ever got her present job' is a noun clause used as the subject of 'was'; 'ever' adds surprise.

sentences.context: Looking at her, you got the feeling that this was someone who could bend iron bars
sentences.simple: When you looked at her, you felt that she was a person who could bend iron bars.
sentences.grammar: 'Looking at her' is a participle phrase meaning 'when you looked at her'; 'who could bend' is a relative clause.

sentences.context: I shall have her for that, you see if I don't
sentences.simple: I will punish her for that. You will see that I do it.
sentences.grammar: 'you see if I don't' is a way to say 'I will certainly do it'; 'shall' is an old, strong way to say 'will'.

sentences.context: I wish to heavens I was still allowed to use the birch and belt
sentences.simple: She wishes she could still use the birch and the belt, as she did in the old days.
sentences.grammar: 'wish + past tense' is used for something you want but do not have now; 'was allowed' is passive.

sentences.context: Sometimes it was well nigh impossible for a teacher to convince the proud father or mother
sentences.simple: Sometimes it was almost impossible for a teacher to make a proud father or mother believe that their loved child was a complete fool.
sentences.grammar: 'it was ... impossible for a teacher to + verb' is a pattern where 'it' stands for the 'to' part; 'well nigh' means 'almost'.

sentences.context: a loud squelching noise similar to that made by a hippopotamus when lowering its foot
sentences.simple: When she sat down in the chair, there was a loud wet noise like the noise a hippopotamus makes when it puts its foot in the mud by the Limpopo River.
sentences.grammar: 'that' stands for 'the noise'; 'made by a hippopotamus' is a past participle phrase, and 'when lowering' is a short form of 'when it lowers'.

sentences.context: the expression on her face was one that you might find on the face of a person
sentences.simple: The girl with the pigtails, Amanda Thripp, stood very still and watched the giant come. The look on her face was a look you might see on a person who is trapped in a small field with a very angry bull that is running at her.
sentences.grammar: 'one' stands for 'expression'; 'that you might find' is a relative clause.

sentences.context: Many were guessing that it had been filled with pepper or castor-oil
sentences.simple: Many children thought that the cake had pepper or castor-oil or something else bad-tasting in it, to make the boy very sick.
sentences.grammar: 'had been filled' is past perfect passive: the filling came before the guessing.

sentences.context: The Trunchbull had as great a dislike for long hair on boys as she had for plaits and pigtails on girls
sentences.simple: The Trunchbull did not like long hair on boys, just as much as she did not like plaits and pigtails on girls. And she was about to show it.
sentences.grammar: 'as great a dislike ... as ...' is an 'as ... as' comparison with a noun; note the word order 'as great a dislike'.

sentences.context: Hurry up or I'll start jerking you up and down
sentences.simple: Be quick. If you are not, I will pull you up and down. Then your hair will really come out, and there will be enough to fill a sofa.
sentences.grammar: An order + 'or' + 'I will ...' means 'if you do not do this, I will do that'.

sentences.context: leapt off her chair as though a firecracker had gone off underneath her
sentences.simple: The Trunchbull jumped off her chair as if a firecracker had gone off under her.
sentences.grammar: 'as though + past perfect' compares with an imagined case that did not really happen.

sentences.context: She didn't in the least mind being accused of having done something she had actually done
sentences.simple: Matilda did not mind at all when people said she had done something that she really had done.
sentences.grammar: 'being accused' is a passive -ing form after 'mind'; 'of having done' is the past form of -ing, for something done earlier.

sentences.context: If they believed her story, and it was doubtful they would, they almost certainly would fail
sentences.simple: It was not likely that they would believe her story. If they did, they almost certainly would not understand what a big thing had happened in the classroom that afternoon.
sentences.grammar: 'If + past, would' is an imagined case; 'it was doubtful they would' leaves out 'believe her story' because it was said just before.

sentences.context: Do any of us children, she wondered, ever stop to ask ourselves where our teachers go
sentences.simple: Matilda wondered if children ever stop and ask where their teachers go after school.
sentences.grammar: 'stop to ask' means stop in order to ask; 'where our teachers go' is a question inside a sentence, so the word order is like a statement.

sentences.context: You were bound to ask in the end
sentences.simple: You were sure to ask at last.
sentences.grammar: 'be bound to + verb' means 'be sure to do something'.

sentences.context: no matter what it was, I obeyed it instantly
sentences.simple: Miss Honey says that over the years she became so afraid of her aunt, and so ruled by her, that she did what her aunt said at once, whatever it was.
sentences.grammar: 'so ... that ...' shows a result; 'no matter what it was' means 'whatever it was'.

sentences.context: she was able not only to lift the cigar up into the air but also to move it around
sentences.simple: She could lift the cigar up into the air. She could also move it around any way she wanted.
sentences.grammar: 'not only ... but also ...' joins two things; both parts have the same form (to lift ... to move).

sentences.context: If there had been, then something exceptionally unpleasant would have happened
sentences.simple: There were no slimy creatures in the water this time. If there had been, something very unpleasant would have happened to every member of the class.
sentences.grammar: 'If + had been, would have + past participle' is about a past case that did not happen.

sentences.context: He'll have been sending his money out there for years
sentences.simple: Miss Honey thinks that for many years he has been sending his money to Spain.
sentences.grammar: 'will have been sending' (future perfect continuous) is used here as a guess: he has been doing it for years up to now.

sentences.context: informing her that the last will and testament of her late father
sentences.simple: The letter told her that her dead father's will had suddenly turned up.
sentences.grammar: 'informing her that ...' is a participle phrase that adds what the letter did; 'had turned up' is past perfect.
